title: Idempotency
subtitle: Doing it twice must equal doing it once — because it will happen twice
objectives: Explain why retries are unavoidable and therefore duplicates are inevitable
Identify which operations are naturally idempotent and which need to be made so
Implement idempotency keys, and account for the state they require
Reason about the boundary: what's idempotent, for how long, and across which systems

exercises.title: A timeout tells you that you stopped waiting — nothing about what the server did
exercises.body: You `POST` a payment. Nothing comes back. The request may never have arrived. Or it arrived, charged the card, and its reply died on the way home. From where you stand these look *exactly* the same. So you get a choice of mistakes: retry and maybe charge twice, or don't and maybe charge nobody.
exercises.note: Idempotency dissolves the choice rather than answering it. Make a repeat harmless and you can always retry — "did it happen?" stops being a question you need answered.

exercises.prompt: You POST a payment. The request times out. Did the charge happen?
choices: No — a timeout means it failed
You cannot tell: the request may never have arrived, or it may have succeeded and the response was lost on the way back
exercises.why: A timeout tells you that you stopped waiting, and nothing whatsoever about what the server did — the failure could be on the way there, during processing, or on the way back with a completed charge behind it. This ambiguity is not a bug in your HTTP client; it's a permanent property of asking anything over a network, and it's the reason this entire unit exists.

exercises.prompt: So what are your two options after that timeout?
choices: Retry and risk charging twice, or don't retry and risk the payment never happening — with no way to know which mistake you're making
Check the logs and retry safely
exercises.why: Both options are guesses about a fact you can't observe, so you're choosing which failure to inflict rather than avoiding failure — double-charge a customer, or silently drop their order. Idempotency is what dissolves the dilemma: make the retry harmless, and you can always retry, which turns an unanswerable question into a non-question.

exercises.prompt: An operation is ______ if performing it many times has the same effect as performing it once.
exercises.why: The word says the outcome is unchanged by repetition — not that the operation refuses to run twice, but that running it twice lands you in the same state as running it once.

exercises.prompt: Where do duplicate requests come from? Select all.
choices: A client retrying after a timeout
A load balancer or proxy retrying a request it thinks failed
exercises.why: All four are routine, and notice how little control you have over most of them — a proxy may retry without telling you, a queue redelivers by design (unit 16), and users click twice because your button didn't respond fast enough. Duplicates aren't an edge case you might hit; they're a standing condition of running a service on a network.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'we'll just be careful not to retry' not a strategy?
choices: It works if the team is disciplined
Because you don't control every retry: browsers, proxies, SDKs, queues, and users all retry independently of your intentions
exercises.why: Your discipline governs your code and nothing else in the path — the mobile SDK, the corporate proxy, and the customer's finger all retry on their own schedules. Since you cannot make duplicates not arrive, the only durable answer is to make arriving twice harmless, which puts the responsibility where you actually have authority: the server.

exercises.prompt: Your service is idempotent. What does that let you do that you couldn't before?
choices: Retry freely — every ambiguous failure becomes safe to resolve by simply trying again
exercises.why: Idempotency converts the unanswerable 'did it happen?' into an irrelevant question: try again and find out, because the retry cannot do harm. That's why it's foundational rather than defensive — reliable distributed systems are built out of retries, and retries are only safe on idempotent operations.

exercises.title: An operation that names a final state repeats harmlessly; one that names a change does not
exercises.body: "Set the balance to 100" can run five times and the balance is 100. "Add 50" runs five times and you're at 250. Absolute intents don't care what came before, so repetition is free; relative and creative intents compound. That's the whole split: `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` name an end state, and `POST` makes something new each call.
exercises.note: *Atomic* and *idempotent* are different words. `UPDATE balance = balance - 10` is perfectly atomic — nothing can interleave with it — and running it twice still takes 20.

exercises.prompt: Match each operation to whether repeating it is safe.

pairs.right: Safe — still deleted the second time
Not safe — creates something new each time

exercises.why: The pattern is that operations naming a final state are repeatable, while operations describing an increment or a creation are not. This is unit 2's methods with the reasoning made explicit: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by their semantics, and POST is the one that isn't.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'set balance to 100' idempotent but 'add 50 to balance' isn't?
choices: 'Set' names an absolute end state, so repeating it lands in the same place; 'add' is relative to whatever is there, so each repeat moves you further
exercises.why: Absolute operations are self-correcting under repetition because they don't care what came before — run 'set 100' five times and it's 100. Relative operations compound, so five retries of 'add 50' is 250. That's a genuine design lever: expressing an intent absolutely rather than relatively can make it idempotent for free, before any keys or bookkeeping.

exercises.prompt: Is `DELETE /users/42` returning 404 on the second call a problem?
choices: Yes — it should return 200 every time
No — the end state is identical (the user is gone), which is what idempotency means; but a retrying client may read 404 as failure, so returning 204 for both is kinder
Yes — it means the delete failed
No, and the status code doesn't matter at all
exercises.why: Idempotency is a claim about state, not about status codes, and the user is equally gone either way — so DELETE is idempotent regardless. But a client can't tell 'already deleted' from 'never existed' if you say 404, and it may escalate a successful retry as an error. Returning 204 for both keeps the state guarantee and makes the retry legible.

exercises.prompt: Your endpoint is `POST /orders`. How could you make it naturally idempotent without any extra bookkeeping?
choices: You can't — POST is never idempotent
Let the client supply the order's id, so a repeat is a create-if-absent on a known key rather than a new row each time
exercises.why: The reason POST isn't idempotent is that the server invents the identity, so every call creates something new — hand identity to the client and the operation becomes 'ensure this specific thing exists', which repeats harmlessly. Note this is the same move as PUT, and a unique constraint on that id makes the database enforce it, which unit 6 taught is the only enforcement that can't be bypassed.

exercises.prompt: Which are naturally idempotent as written? Select all.
choices: UPDATE users SET email='x' WHERE id=42
`UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1` WHERE id=42
exercises.why: Setting an absolute value, inserting-if-absent, and deleting a specific row all land in the same state however many times they run. The increment is the odd one out and it's worth noticing why: unit 6 recommended 'n = n + 1' as the fix for lost updates, and it's atomic — but atomic and idempotent are different properties, and a retried increment counts twice.

exercises.prompt: So what's the first question to ask about any write?
choices: If this ran twice, would the end state differ — and can I express the intent absolutely instead of relatively?
exercises.why: Asking it early is cheap and often free: a lot of operations can be made idempotent purely by how you phrase them, before you build any machinery. Only when the intent is genuinely creative or relative — charge this card, send this email — do you need keys and stored results, which is the next lesson and the expensive path.

exercises.title: An idempotency key names the *intent*, so every retry of one charge arrives under the same name
exercises.body: The client mints a unique key before its first attempt and reuses it on every retry of that same intent. The server's first move — before any work — is to insert that key atomically, insert-if-absent. Win the insert: do the work, then store the result under the key. Lose it: the key is already claimed, so return what's stored.
exercises.note: Look the key up and *then* decide, and you've written check-then-act. Two simultaneous retries both look, both find nothing, both charge. The store's unique constraint must pick the winner — not your `if`.

exercises.prompt: `POST /payments` genuinely creates a charge. How do you make retrying it safe?
choices: Check whether a similar payment exists recently
The client generates a unique key per intended payment and sends it; the server records that key with its result and returns the original result if the key reappears
Add a timestamp and reject duplicates within a second
exercises.why: The key names the INTENT rather than the request, so all retries of one intended charge carry the same key and the server can recognise them as the same act. 'Similar payment recently' is a heuristic that fails both ways — it blocks a customer legitimately buying the same coffee twice, and it misses a retry that arrives late.

exercises.prompt: Order the server's handling of a request with an idempotency key.
steps: Receive the request with key K
Atomically insert K as in-progress — the store's unique constraint picks the winner
If that insert conflicts, K was already claimed: return the stored result, or wait if it's still in progress
If the insert won, do the work
Update K with the result before responding
exercises.why: The trick is step 2. Reserving the key atomically BEFORE doing the work is what makes two simultaneous retries resolve to exactly one winner — the store's uniqueness constraint arbitrates, and the loser is told K already exists rather than finding nothing. Looking the key up and then acting on what you found is check-then-act, the same race from unit 6, and under concurrency it double-charges: both retries look, both find nothing, both proceed. That matters because a timeout typically triggers the client's retry AND a proxy's retry at once, so the concurrent case is the normal case rather than the exotic one.

exercises.prompt: Why must the key be generated by the CLIENT, not the server?
choices: Clients have better random number generators
Because the key must be identical across retries — a server-generated key would be new on each attempt, which is exactly what you're trying to prevent
exercises.why: The key's only job is to be the same on every retry of one intent, and only the client knows that two attempts are the same intent — the server sees two indistinguishable requests. So the client mints the key once, before the first attempt, and reuses it for every retry of that attempt. A key generated per-request would make every retry look brand new.

exercises.prompt: Two retries of the same key arrive simultaneously and both find no existing record. What happens?
choices: Both proceed and you charge twice: your idempotency check is check-then-act, which is a race unless the key store enforces uniqueness atomically
exercises.why: This is unit 6's check-then-act race living inside the very mechanism meant to prevent duplicates — and it's the bug that makes an idempotency implementation look correct until traffic is concurrent. The fix is the same: let the store enforce uniqueness on the key with an atomic insert, so one attempt wins and the other sees the conflict rather than an empty result.

exercises.prompt: The idempotency store is itself state. What does it demand?
choices: Durability (surviving a crash mid-payment), sharing across all servers (any one may get the retry), and expiry (or it grows forever)
It must be in memory for performance
exercises.why: Unit 5's question applied to the key store gives brutal answers: lose it and you lose the record of what you already did, so it must be durable; the retry may hit any server, so it must be shared; and it accumulates a row per intent forever, so it needs a retention policy. This is why idempotency isn't free — 'make it reliable' meant 'add state, in the right place', and here the state is as critical as the payments themselves.

exercises.prompt: You expire idempotency keys after 24 hours. A client retries after 25. What happens?
choices: The key is gone, so it looks like a brand-new request and you charge again — your guarantee has a time limit you chose
The key is restored from backup
exercises.why: Retention length IS the length of your guarantee, so 'idempotent' silently means 'idempotent for 24 hours' — and that's a real window someone's dead-letter replay can walk right through. The window has to outlive your longest plausible retry path, including a human rerunning a failed batch on Monday morning, or the promise quietly stops holding exactly when it's most needed.

exercises.title: Idempotency covers exactly what the key covers, and not one thing more
exercises.body: You deduplicated the charge. The confirmation email was never in the deal. A retry re-runs every side effect living outside the key's record — the email, the third-party call, the event you published. Your database can be spotless while the customer reads two receipts and a downstream service does the work twice.
exercises.note: Anything that leaves your database can't be rolled back; the world remembers. Each side effect is its own promise: fire it once from the stored result, or hand it a key of its own.

exercises.prompt: Your payment endpoint is idempotent. It also sends a confirmation email. A retry arrives. What does the customer get?
choices: Possibly two — the charge was deduplicated, but the email was a side effect that may have fired on both attempts unless it's covered by the same key
exercises.why: Idempotency protects whatever the key covers and nothing else, so a side effect performed outside that record happily runs again. The fix is to make the stored result the boundary — record the outcome and fire effects from it once, or hand the email its own key. Every side effect is a separate promise, and each needs deciding.

exercises.prompt: Which are side effects that need their own idempotency thought? Select all.
choices: Publishing an event other services consume
Reading a row to build the response
exercises.why: Emails, external calls, and published events all reach outside your database and can't be rolled back — a retry that re-fires them is visible to customers or triggers downstream work twice. The read is harmless because it changes nothing, which is the whole distinction: side effects are the things the world remembers.

exercises.prompt: Your idempotency store is in your database; the payment goes to Stripe. You record the key, then call Stripe, then crash. What state are you in?
choices: Ambiguous: the key says you started, but you don't know whether Stripe charged — so the retry sees the key and may return a result you never actually confirmed
exercises.why: This is unit 9's boundary again — your database and Stripe cannot commit together — so recording the key and doing the work are two steps with a crash-shaped hole between them. Which is why the mature pattern stores the key as in-progress first, then reconciles: on retry you see 'started but unconfirmed' and go ask Stripe what actually happened, using YOUR key as the identifier you gave them.

exercises.prompt: Why does Stripe accept an `Idempotency-Key` header from you?
choices: Because they know your retries are unavoidable, so they let you name the intent and guarantee that one key charges once — pushing the guarantee to where the side effect actually happens
exercises.why: The only place a charge can truly be deduplicated is at the system that performs it, so Stripe offers the guarantee at the boundary where it's enforceable. The general principle is worth taking: an API that performs irreversible side effects should accept an idempotency key, because its callers will retry whether it's safe or not.

exercises.prompt: You're designing a public API that creates resources. Slide toward your approach to duplicate protection.
exercises.why: Heuristics guess at intent and are wrong in both directions — they block a customer genuinely ordering the same thing twice, and they miss a retry that arrives outside the window. A key is unambiguous because the client states 'this is the same intent as before', which is the one fact only the client knows. Explicit intent beats inferred intent every time you can get it.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of idempotency?
choices: It's a nice-to-have for payment systems
It's what makes retries safe — and since retries are unavoidable, it's what makes reliability possible at all. It costs you durable, shared, expiring state, and it only covers what the key covers
It means an operation runs only once
exercises.why: You cannot tell whether a timed-out request happened, so either retries are safe or your system is guessing about money — that's why this is foundational rather than defensive. And it's bounded in three ways worth naming out loud: it lasts as long as your retention, it covers only the operations you keyed, and it stops at every system boundary you don't control.
